lead: Adsorption is a surface operation. Molecules of a solute leave a fluid and stick to the outside and inside surface of a porous solid. The fluid is the feed; the solid is the adsorbent; the stuck solute is the adsorbate. The solid is not dissolved and its structure barely changes. Industries use adsorption to remove colour from sugar, polish drinking water, recover solvent vapour, dry air and separate oxygen from air. The solid's surface area and pore size decide how much it can hold and how fast it works.
prereq: You need diffusion ideas from Unit 1, Molecular Diffusion and Diffusivity, and interphase transfer from Unit 2, Mass Transfer Coefficients and Interphase Transfer; 6.2 adds equilibrium isotherms.

blocks.text: Adsorption happens at an interface. The solid offers a surface; the fluid touches it. A solute molecule that sticks is the adsorbate. The solid that holds it is the adsorbent. The word adsorption is not absorption: absorption takes solute into the bulk of another phase, as in gas absorption (see Unit 3). Adsorption keeps solute on the surface, though the surface may be inside pores.

Physical adsorption, also called van der Waals adsorption in some syllabi, uses weak forces. It is reversible, gives low heat, and gets weaker as temperature rises. Chemical adsorption, or chemisorption, forms a chemical bond. It is stronger, gives high heat, and may need activation energy. A real adsorbent can show both, depending on solute and conditions.

The path has three resistances. Solute first crosses the film of fluid around the particle: film diffusion. It then moves through pore mouths and along pore walls: pore diffusion. Finally it attaches to an active site: surface adsorption. Any step can be slow, but the last step supplies the capacity.

Capacity is reported as q, mass of adsorbate per mass of dry adsorbent, usually mg/g. A gram of good activated carbon can expose more than 1000 m² of surface; that is roughly a football field. The area is mostly inside pores. More area means more sites and higher q at the same fluid concentration.

Pore size sets a trade-off. Micropores are under 2 nm, mesopores are 2–50 nm, macropores are above 50 nm. Micropores give high area and hold small molecules strongly, but diffusion is slow. Macropores give fast access but little area. A useful solid has a pore network: large pores as roads, small pores as storage rooms.

Pressure and temperature change the equilibrium qualitatively. For a gas, higher pressure pushes more molecules onto the surface. For physical adsorption, higher temperature gives molecules more energy to escape, so loading falls. Chemisorption can behave differently because a bond must form. The full q against C curve is the isotherm; 6.2 treats its equations.

Activated carbon is made by heating carbon-rich material such as coconut shell or coal without air, then activating with steam or chemicals. It has high area, is non-polar, and adsorbs organic vapours, dyes, colour and many trace pollutants. It is used in water treatment and solvent recovery.

Silica gel is porous silicon dioxide. It is polar and holds water strongly, so it dries air and gases. Activated alumina is porous aluminium oxide; it also dries gases and removes fluoride and some ions. Zeolites are crystalline aluminosilicates with uniform pores. They act as molecular sieves: a molecule that is too large cannot enter. They separate oxygen from nitrogen and dry gases.

Ion-exchange resins are polymer beads with charged groups. They take ions from solution and release other ions of the same charge. The surface holds the ions, so the unit links to 6.4. Resins are not high-area carbons, but they are selective. Softening hard water and demineralising water use them.

examples.question: 2.00 g activated carbon is shaken with 100 mL of dye solution. The initial dye concentration is 50 mg/L and the final equilibrium concentration is 10 mg/L. Find the adsorption capacity q in mg/g.
steps: List the data: C<sub>0</sub> = 50 mg/L, C<sub>e</sub> = 10 mg/L, V = 100 mL, W = 2.00 g.
Convert the volume: V = 100 mL × (1 L / 1000 mL) = 0.100 L.
Dye removed = (C<sub>0</sub> − C<sub>e</sub>)V = (50 − 10) mg/L × 0.100 L = 40 × 0.100 = 4.0 mg.
q = removed mass ÷ adsorbent mass = 4.0 mg ÷ 2.00 g = 2.0 mg/g.
examples.answer: The adsorption capacity is q = 2.0 mg/g.
examples.check:
C0 = 50.0
Ce = 10.0
V_mL = 100.0
W = 2.00
V_L = V_mL / 1000.0
removed = (C0 - Ce) * V_L
q = removed / W
print(q)

traps: Using V = 100 directly with mg/L gives 4000 mg, not 4.0 mg; convert mL to L first.
Writing q as mg per litre of solution; q is mg per gram of dry adsorbent.
Mixing adsorption with absorption; adsorption is surface-held, absorption enters the bulk.
Assuming chemisorption is always reversible like physisorption; chemisorption forms bonds and may need heat to reverse.
Using the initial concentration as the equilibrium value; q needs the final equilibrium concentration C<sub>e</sub>.

quiz.a: Adsorbate is the solute held on the surface; adsorbent is the porous solid that holds it.

quiz.q: Why does high surface area raise adsorption capacity?
quiz.a: More area exposes more active sites, so more adsorbate can attach per gram at the same fluid concentration.

quiz.q: 5.00 g carbon is shaken with 250 mL of solution. C<sub>0</sub> = 80 mg/L and C<sub>e</sub> = 20 mg/L. Find q in mg/g.
Small pores raise area but slow uptake. Explain the design trade-off.
quiz.a: Micropores store more adsorbate but make diffusion slow. A network with macropores feeding micropores gives fast access and high capacity.

quiz.q: Give two differences between physical and chemical adsorption.
quiz.a: Physical adsorption uses weak van der Waals forces, gives low heat, and is usually reversible. Chemical adsorption forms bonds, gives high heat, and may need activation energy.

quiz.q: Why can a zeolite separate oxygen from nitrogen when both molecules are small?
quiz.a: Zeolite pores are uniform and near molecular size; one molecule enters faster or is held more strongly by polar sites, giving a kinetic or equilibrium separation.

quiz.q: A gas adsorber is warmed at constant pressure. What happens to physical adsorption loading?
quiz.a: Physical adsorption is exothermic; warming shifts equilibrium toward desorption, so loading falls.

quiz.q: Name two adsorbents used for drying gases.
quiz.a: Silica gel and activated alumina; zeolites also dry gases.

beyond: Not for the exam. Pressure-swing adsorption uses zeolites or carbon to make oxygen from air and hydrogen from reformer gas; the bed is regenerated by dropping pressure, not by heat. Water treatment uses granular activated carbon and ion-exchange resins in fixed beds. Research adsorbents include metal-organic frameworks with very high area and tuned pores, and biochar from farm waste. Search terms: pressure-swing adsorption, molecular sieve, activated carbon breakthrough, metal-organic framework adsorption.
